question: In November 2022, the health authorities of the Autonomous Community of Valencia awarded a contract of more than EUR 4 million for the purchase of three mobile electron accelerators for intraoperative radiotherapy in breast cancer, with the aim of improving local accessibility in hospitals in Valencia, Elche and Castellón, setting a delivery time of six months.
Long after that deadline, only one of the three machines is operational. This state of affairs creates unacceptable inequalities in access to quality cancer treatment.

Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan and the Commission’s latest report recognises that inequality between countries and between regions remains in access to timely diagnostics and treatments, undermining standards of care and territorial fairness within the Union. In view of the above: 1.
How is the Commission monitoring regional inequalities in access to cancer diagnoses and treatment in practice, and what measures is it taking to address them?

What instruments can the Commission use to take action when public procurement procedures for medical devices subject to EU law lead to significant delays that may exacerbate territorial inequalities in cancer care?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.2.2026) The European Cancer Inequalities Registry is a flagship of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan, supporting the monitoring of inequalities across the cancer care pathway, including regional data on mortality.

By providing data through a data tool1, Country Cancer Profiles2 and EU analytical reports3, the Registry highlights gaps and potential targeted areas, to help national and regional governments to direct investments and interventions. Where possible, the Profiles also analyse regional inequalities in access to care, distribution of workforce and medical resources.

The Commission is taking measures to support Member States and stakeholders in addressing these inequalities, including through EU4Health Programme funding. In screening, the Joint Action EUCanScreen4 set up a work package to coordinate and support activities reducing inequalities in access to and quality of breast, cervical and colorectal cancer screening and care services.

Recent calls for proposals on lung, prostate and gastric cancer screening5 provide for the mandatory inclusion of an equity perspective. In treatment, the Joint Action ‘European network of Comprehensive Cancer Centres’ (EUnetCCC)6 has a strong equality focus with its goal of 90% of eligible patients having access to high-quality care in a Comprehensive Cancer Centre, regardless of where they live.

Concerning procurement, the EU public procurement rules (namely the procurement Directives when the procurement is launched at the national level like in Valencia’s case) govern the procedure for the award of public contracts and concession contracts.
In contrast, the performance of these contracts, in particular regarding the fulfilment of a contractor’s obligations, is a matter for the National Contracting Authority.
